<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Section 15(a)(1)(C) of the Small Business Act states that the Small Business Administration (SBA) shall ``assur[e] that a fair proportion of the total purchases and contracts for goods and services of the Government . . . are awarded to small business concerns.''\1\ The main authority federal agencies use to create a level playing field for small businesses is to set aside contracts for small business-only competitions. Contracting officers can, and in some cases must, exclude other-than-small firms from participation, therefore allowing small businesses to compete with firms of similar size and scale while maintaining the competitive requirements in the Competition in Contracting Act.
\1\15 U.S.C. 644(a)(1)(C).
Currently, the Small Business Act requires that federal agencies default to small business set asides for contracts with values under the Simplified Acquisition Threshold (SAT/ $350,000), unless there is not a reasonable expectation that two small businesses can and will make competitive offers. For contracts above the SAT, contracting officers must conduct market research and determine if there are two or more responsible small businesses that will make offers and can perform the work at fair market prices.\2\ If contracting officers have a reasonable expectation that offers will be received from two or more small businesses, they must set the contracts aside and allow only small businesses to compete. This analysis is known as the ``Rule of Two'' and is the process that triggers small business competition.
\2\13 CFR 125.2(f); 48 CFR 19.502-2.
The Rule of Two has been a regulatory requirement for forty years and is the foundation of the Federal Government's support for small business prime contracting. The requirement for a Rule of Two analysis was put in place in recognition of the fact that if small businesses were required to compete with large corporations, it would be nearly impossible for any small business to win a contract, let alone be awarded a ``fair proportion.'' This is especially true for small businesses seeking federal contracts for the first time.
The data bears this out: with the Rule of Two in place, over $100 billion dollars is now awarded annually to small business government contractors through small business-only competitions. In fiscal year 2024 alone, $72 billion was awarded through general small business set-asides.\3\ That does not include contracts awarded through one of SBA's procurement programs--which this legislation protects and enables.
\3\U.S. Small Bus. Admin., Final FY23 Corrective Action Report with Agency Reports and Addenda, (Sep. 9, 2024) and Small Business Data HUB. https://datahub.certify.sba.gov/ (last accessed Apr. 24, 2026).
The Rule of Two has been retained during changes to federal procurement regulations since its initial inclusion in the Federal Acquisition Regulations (FAR) 40 years ago. On April 15, 2025, the President issued Executive Order (EO) 14275 requiring the government to review and rewrite the FAR, initiating the most recent round of reviews.\4\ The newest version of the FAR retained the Rule of Two. However, both EO 14275 and the revised FAR (which has not yet moved through the formal rulemaking process) include a section that stated any provision retained in the revision, but not based on statute, would expire in four years unless extended by the FAR Council.\5\ As a result, the Rule of Two's future as a regulatory requirement is less secure.
\4\Exec. Order No. 14275, 90 Fed. Reg. 16447 (Apr. 15, 2025).
\5\FAR Part 1.109: ``All FAR sections that are not required by statute must expire 4 years after the effective date of the sections, unless renewed by the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council.''
The Committee believes that retaining and codifying the Rule of Two must be a top priority and has consistently and publicly highlighted the need to do so since the signing of EO 14275--including through hearing records, press releases, op-eds, and outreach to the community. This effort has demonstrated the overwhelming support among the small business community for retaining the Rule of Two and enacting H.R. 2804. The Protecting Small Business Competitions Act is formally endorsed by more than 35 organizations and hundreds of small businesses.
For example, the Committee record includes testimony from a September 10, 2025, Small Business Subcommittee on Contracting and Infrastructure hearing entitled: ``Leveling the Playing Field: Fostering Opportunities for Small Business Contractors,'' which discussed the FAR rewrite and the necessity of retaining the Rule of Two. The witnesses invited by both sides of the aisle highlighted the need to codify the Rule of Two and the strong, bipartisan support for doing so. Ms. Sue Tellier stated: ``The Rule of Two has historically been a bedrock protection for us. Its erosion results in a less welcoming environment--reducing opportunities for small innovative firms and instead accelerating consolidation.'' Mr. Michael Ramos stated: ``If we remove the Rule of Two, that will be damaging to the defense industrial base. I think that's pretty critical to understand. If you remove that rule and you do not codify it, you have this scenario where not only will [small businesses] leave, but you will just create massive entrenchment of the existing larger small businesses.''\6\
\6\Leveling the Playing Field: Fostering Opportunities for Small Business Contractors. Hearing before the H. COMM. ON SMALL BUS., 119th Cong. (2025).
The purpose of H.R. 2804 is to codify the current requirement and application of the Rule of Two as included in the Federal Acquisition Regulation, while retaining and preserving the existing exemptions, including those found in the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul's 19.104-1. H.R. 2804 does not expand the Rule of Two to procurements outside of its current application. In particular, procurements governed by different laws and processes, such as procurements made pursuant to the Javits-Wagner-O'Day Act (41 U.S.C. 8501, et seq.), or current, specific requirements at federal agencies, are not covered by H.R. 2804.
Preserving and codifying the Rule of Two as applied today will ensure that both small business competitions and other important procurement programs and structures remain consistent with the purpose of their enactment. For example, non-competitive procurements--including acquisitions with a statutorily mandated source such as Federal Prison Industries or AbilityOne--or procurement processes with alternative structures--such as procurement conducted for Architect and Engineering services via the Brooks Act, and small business direct award authorities--have been deliberately and specifically crafted to ensure the industrial base can efficiently support agency missions while realistically supporting Congressionally directed policy objectives. Among other objectives, Congress has directed federal agencies to use specific authorities--through mandatory and competitive procurements--to promote American's small business (contracts set-aside for small business competitions), American products and services (ie: Buy America Act) and American jobs (AbilityOne and competitions restricted to small firms in HUBZones). This bill does not repeal any existing laws and retains, codifies and protects that structure in statute for the future.
Similarly, the Committee adopted an Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute to remove the underlying bill's expansion of the Rule or Two's applicability to task and delivery orders. On January 15, 2025, the FAR Council issued a proposed rule to increase small business participation on certain multiple-award contracts by among other provisions, expanding the Rule of Two to placement of task and delivery orders.\7\ At the time of introduction of H.R. 2804, this rule remained in the proposed rule stage, and therefore, the bill's text included ``contracts, task order and delivery orders.'' The proposed rule was withdrawn on June 12, 2025\8\ and no expansion of the Rule of Two was included in changes made by the FAR Council.
\7\90 Fed. Reg. 3753 (Jan. 15, 2025).
\8\90 Fed. Reg. 24773 (Jun. 12, 2025).
The bill, as amended and passed, aligns with the current acquisition regulations regarding the applicability of the Rule of Two to task and delivery orders.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
